newsitem.title: CHINA: Deng's Beijing memorial poses security challenge.
newsitem.headline: Deng's Beijing memorial poses security challenge.

text.p: The last time China held a memorial for a Communist Party luminary, 50,000 students came uninvited to mass in silence outside -- a bold act of dissent that swelled into the 1989 Tiananmen democracy protests.

That outcome, sparked by the funeral of disgraced former Communist Party chief Hu Yaobang, is something Beijing will go to extremes to prevent when 10,000 carefully chosen guests attend Tuesday's memorial for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
Security was already tight on Friday in Tiananmen Square near the Great Hall of the People where the memorial will be held.
A man carrying a memorial wreath was seized by plainclothes police and bundled into a car, witnesses said.
Security also is sure to be tight to the west of town at the Communist Party's hallowed Babaoshan Cemetery, where Deng's private cremation is likely to be held.
The Supreme People's Court, China's top judicial body, on Friday ordered all courts to ensure strict law enforcement and to safeguard social stability.
Deng's successors will leave little to chance in a country where public mourning has a habit of spiralling into protest.
China's constitution guarantees the rights of free speech and assembly, but citizens in reality have few ways to vent frustration in public.

On April 5, 1976, the removal of wreaths placed in Tiananmen Square to memorialise the late Premier Zhou Enlai sparked protests against Mao Zedong's "gang of four" lieutenants, who had conducted the ultra-leftist Cultural Revolution since 1966.
Many participants were arrested, but the September 8 death of Mao led to a purge of the gang a month later, enabling Deng to emerge from political limbo.
The outcome was far more dramatic 13 years later.

Immediately after the April 15, 1989, death of Hu Yaobang -- who had been sacked two years earlier for abetting Western values -- students seized the moment to hail a man they saw as a champion of political liberalisation.
Initial placarding on campus soon escalated to marches by hundreds of students mourning Hu's death but also denouncing official corruption, inflation and the poor lot of students.

On the eve of Hu's memorial, an estimated 100,000 people massed in Tiananmen Square. Remnants of these stayed through the night to be there when the official mourning began, and the crowd soon swelled again to 50,000.
Hundreds of police failed to drive them back and their demands to meet Premier Li Peng were turned down.

Silence fell over the throng as the 20-minute memorial began, but soon the students massed at the foot of the Great Hall's broad stairs were singing the Internationale, the world communist anthem, and chanting "dialogue, dialogue".
The Communist Party leadership inside gave no public reply.
Within a day after the students' rebuff, rioting broke out in Xian and other provincial capitals and indignant students organised campus strikes and protest rallies in many cities.

Emboldened by the lack of a forceful response, organisers mounted new waves of protests and eventually occupied the vast square in the most serious challenge of communist rule since the party seized power in 1949.
Deng finally ordered the mass protests crushed. The People's Liberation Army rolled through Beijing guns ablaze on June 3-4 in a crackdown that killed hundreds and indelibly marred Deng's legacy.
